799.t: Lessons with Santo Giuffre, Eddie Miller and a musical family
799.s: Studied with Giuffre, taught Eddie Miller what he learned, and later taught Giuffre saxophone; mother and sisters were musical; Giuffre's solfege training.
799.q: It seems like as though I came up just during the shift, just before the shift to the BAME you see. And I was playing for about three years and I decided to learn how to read music so I went to an old Professor Giuffre here.

799.t: Study under Giuffre and his clarinetist son Philip
799.s: Two years with Giuffre using the Klose method, his strict teaching, and his son Dr. Philip Giuffre who played superbly.
799.q: And I went through that clozé method, which was about an inch and a half thick, you know. Clozé? Clozé, clarinet method. It's a complete method. It's a great big thing. And after you go through that thing boy, you've done some playing. And the old man, Jewfree, was a stickler. He had a baton and he…

641.t: First teacher Manuel Roque; New Orleans bands at his father's shop
641.s: Manuel Roque, a bricklayer from New Orleans, was his first clarinet teacher; visiting bands had their shoes fixed by his father, who knew Alphonse Picou.
641.ch: Clarinet teachers and the Baton Rouge scene
641.q: Manuel Roque was my first clarinet teacher. Incidentally, he was from New Orleans, but he settled in Baton Rouge. Every time one of the bands from

641.t: Free clarinet lessons from Isadore Fritz
641.s: Joe kept studying with Roque while Fritz, a Standard Oil worker, showed him things for free when he visited his father.
641.ch: Clarinet teachers and the Baton Rouge scene
641.q: I never did quit Manuel Roque. I learned more or less from both of them. But the only difference was I didn't have to pay Fritz.

917.t: What became of Freddie's cornet; Keppard's own lessons
917.s: Keppard holds Freddie's first little cornet; Herb Moran bought the later one from Freddie's wife. Keppard himself got cornet lessons from Mal Perez and Hippolyte Charles.
917.q: Well, I got his little cornet now. You don't have it now? No. He went to Chicago with the cornet and then he bought a new cornet. And this fellow here, just remember what he was for, he's dead now. But he's lived.

921.t: Teaching Albert Nicholas and Harold's boyhood
921.s: Her father taught Albert Nicholas reading twice a week after the Navy; Harold recalls living near St. Philip as a boy and his own early job.
921.q: My daddy used to play all out in Chicago and, um, South Carolina. Anywhere. Just anywhere. He traveled all over. A lot of travel.

174.t: Lessons with Nickerson and Lorenzo Tio
174.s: He began lessons at eight or nine with Professor Nickerson, then Lorenzo Tio, from whom he really learned to read and play.
174.q: Yeah, good old days. I started taking lessons on him, about eight or nine years old or something like that. Who was your teacher? Well, first I went to Professor Nickerson because Lorenzo Teal was in New York. And my brother was supposed to go to Mary Perez, and Mary Perez in New York, so he went…

251.t: Lessons with Papa Tio and quitting after misreading Bigard's nose
251.s: He briefly studied fundamentals with the old clarinet teacher Tio, left thinking cousin Barney Bigard was laughing at him, and then his father found Mr. Piron.
251.q: So one brother is still living there. He's still living, but I don't remember him. But the one that finished, well, anyhow, Bonnie went to, he says, well, come on, Papa, I'll take you over. So I went over to one day with him. And Bonnie took his lessons first. Then after he went through his, he was…

12.s: Nicholas names the four major Tio students: Jimmy Noone, himself, Barney Bigard and Omer Simeon.
12.q: Yeah, yeah. Jimmy Noon was ahead of me. I was second, and Barney Begard and Omar Simeon. Omar Simeon, he was in Chicago. And those were, we were the four major students of Tio.

1039.t: First lesson, the Johnny Dodds remark and the F exercise
1039.s: Bechet had him play, then gave a first exercise in F in the low register on fifths and thirds. Bechet did not think much of Johnny Dodds as a musician.
1039.q: Well, he asked me to play something on the clarinet, and I played it very badly, of course. So then I came back, and he gave me a lesson.

291.t: Teachers: brother taught clarinet, a few lessons from Theo
291.s: He was mostly self-taught, with a few lessons from Theo, who helped on saxophone; his brother taught him clarinet.
291.q: Um, practically self-learned. Because I had taken, what, three or four lessons from Miranda Theo. But he was always high all the time, so I didn't bother him. I just went right on. Studied and self-learned.

849.t: Cheap lessons with an old teacher on St. Gloria Street
849.s: He took two-bit lessons from a strict teacher who made pupils hum notes and answer theory questions before touching the horn.
849.q: Well, you come from, you know, come from school sometime. I wasn't there two bits to go play. I lied to my aunt and went to music lessons. Same time I didn't go. He's right there on St. Gloria Street. Old man Shao Ney. He learned white in color too. White in color. He was a good old teacher. See,…

366.s: Bellison, who taught Goodman too, refused jazz players; Sol commuted from Brooklyn to the Bronx for lessons.
366.q: The teacher I went to, I don’t know if you saw it in the article I gave you, Monk, his name was Simeon Bellison. He played clarinet with the New York Philharmonic for 40 years. Number one, if he knew you played saxophone, which I did not play saxophone, he wouldn’t teach you. If he knew you played…
